A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same lattice-transform compression work. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B and D report original Gaussian, Physics, and Speech experiments, ablations, and empirical sliced-Wasserstein estimates.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices C and E retain original compression experiments and statistical-distance estimates, and add MNIST results.

M1.justification: Definitions 3.2 and 3.4 introduce a scale s for the private decoder dither: PD-LTC changes from gs(yhat+u) to gs(yhat+su), and QSD-LTC similarly scales its private fine-lattice dither. This is a limited procedural generalization; SD-LTC and the basic training objectives remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains Gaussian, Physics, and Speech evaluation and adds compression of 28-by-28 MNIST images. This extends evaluation from low-dimensional synthetic and measurement/audio vectors to a substantially higher-dimensional image domain.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same deterministic, private-dither, shared-dither, and quantized-shared-dither NTC/LTC comparisons, including nesting ratios 2 and 3. Gaussian comparisons still include RCC at dimensions 1 and 8. MNIST extends the existing comparator family; rearranged main-text plots do not remove comparisons retained in the appendices.

E3.justification: The added MNIST protocol uses latent dimension 8 and discriminator-based test Wasserstein evaluation (Appendix B). Section 5.2 also changes the stated lattice assignments from Speech/E8 and Physics/Lambda16 to Physics/E8 and Speech/Lambda16. Since v1's Speech ablation already uses Lambda16, this reported correction does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The Speech lattice-choice and STE-versus-noisy-proxy ablations are retained, moving from v1 Figures 12–13 to v2 Figures 11–12. The sliced-Wasserstein validation with 20 and 50 projections is also retained. MNIST adds benchmark evidence without a distinct new ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 retain identical estimates and standard errors. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and v2 adds no repeated-run or training-seed information.

E6.justification: v2 adds a full set of MNIST rate-distortion and rate-perception outcomes across the NTC/LTC and dithering variants (Figures 5–6 and 8). The existing Physics, Speech, RCC, ablation, and sliced-Wasserstein results are retained. The substantive empirical addition is image-compression evidence, rather than a demonstrated same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: v1 Theorem 4.6 claims achievability of Rp(D,0), below R(D/2,infinity). v2 Theorem 4.5 replaces this with optimality at R(D/2,infinity). Appendix D introduces explicit flatness-factor conditions, achievable-region bounds in Lemma D.5, revised Wasserstein arguments, a polar-lattice construction, and an extension to perfect perception. Proposition 3.3 is also generalized to scaled dithering.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion change from Gaussian optimality for SD-LTC alone to optimality for both SD-LTC and PD-LTC. The private-randomness contribution changes meaning: v1 claims a rate strictly better than the twice-distortion limit, whereas v2 claims attainment of that limit under perfect or near-perfect perception.

C2.justification: v2 withdraws the interpretation that Gaussian experiments support R(D/2,infinity) not being the private-randomness limit. It explains why sufficiently large private dithers must extend outside lattice cells and specifies the relevant flatness-factor requirements. It also adds a limitation concerning integration with image-compression hyperpriors that implicitly use deterministic dithering.

D1.justification: New Appendix B specifies factorized entropy densities for NTC, RealNVP densities for LTC, 100 training epochs, test-split averaging, and an NVIDIA RTX5000 GPU. These are newly documented settings, not demonstrated changes to existing experiments. Previously stated linear-transform and MLP details are relocated; the empirical choice of the new dither scale s remains unspecified.

R1.justification: The private-randomness contribution is repositioned as attaining an established limit, with Yan et al. (2021) newly cited, rather than achieving a rate below the twice-distortion benchmark. Section 2 also credits Saldi et al. (2015) with the earlier perfect-perception coding theorem, revising v1's attribution to Theis and Wagner (2021). New polar-lattice and optimal-transport references support the revised proof.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively condensed and rewritten. Numbered related-work subsections become thematic paragraphs, much RCC background moves to Appendix A, experimental details are consolidated in new Appendix B, and the private-randomness proof is reorganized around explicit lemmas. These changes extend beyond scientific additions and renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to one row. The standalone Gaussian-limit plot is removed, a new latent-channel schematic is added, and the real-world comparisons are regrouped into multi-dataset grids incorporating MNIST. Appendix plots and ablation panels are resized and rearranged, with substantially denser figure layouts.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the revised private-randomness argument: v1's below-limit claim and unqualified total-variation-to-Wasserstein step are replaced by explicit dither scaling, flatness-factor conditions, and moment-controlled Wasserstein bounds in Appendix D. This addresses important gaps in a central contribution. MNIST results and implementation disclosures add useful support. Denser figures and the unspecified empirical choice of s remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in theoretical justification.
